abstract: The OECD Skills Outlook 2025 examines how countries can build 21st-century skills for all, drawing on the 2023 Survey of Adult Skills. The report finds that differences in education and skills between adults with advantaged and disadvantaged backgrounds explain a large share of the wage gap, and that workers with strong numeracy skills reap disproportionately large wage returns from further upskilling. It argues that as AI handles routine information-processing, human value creation increasingly hinges on creative engagement with ambiguous challenges.
keyFindings: Adults with parents who completed tertiary degrees earn 11% more, but this premium falls to less than 1% when comparing adults with similar educational attainment and skills.
Women earn about 14% less per hour than men, widening to 17% among adults with comparable education and skills.
Individuals in information/communications, financial/insurance, and real estate can expect to earn around 19% more than similar individuals in administrative/support service activities.
Workers with strong numeracy skills reap disproportionately large wage returns from further upskilling.
Generative AI technologies may help reduce disparities in cognitive ability by automating routine intellectual tasks, according to recent research cited in the report.
methodology: 264-page OECD report published December 2025, drawing primarily on the 2023 Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) across member countries. Analyzes literacy, numeracy, and adaptive problem-solving skills across demographic groups with cross-country comparative methodology.
qualifiers: The report focuses on OECD member countries. Wage returns to skills are largely independent of a worker's broader skills profile when comparing individuals with similar socio-demographic characteristics. The relationship between AI adoption and skills demand is evolving faster than policy cycles, introducing uncertainty into projections.
